cards.front: Recall a key point about Market Failure
cards.back: Market failure occurs when the market system fails to allocate resources efficiently — the price mechanism produces the wrong quantity of a good.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Market Failure
cards.back: Externalities are costs or benefits affecting third parties not involved in the transaction. Social cost = private cost + external cost. Social benefit = private benefit + external benefit.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Market Failure
cards.back: Negative externalities: pollution from a factory harms nearby residents (costs not reflected in price). Over-production and over-consumption result.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Market Failure
cards.back: Positive externalities: education benefits society beyond the individual (lower crime, higher productivity). Under-consumption and under-production result.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Market Failure
cards.back: Government intervention to correct market failure: taxes (on negative externalities), subsidies (for positive externalities), regulation (banning harmful activities), and providing public goods directly.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating market failure, use the SPICE framework: Social cost vs private cost? Is there an externality? Can government Correct it? Effectiveness of intervention? Which policy works best?
Social cost exceeds private cost (e.g. Over-production)
Social benefit exceeds private benefit (e.g. Under-production)
Non-excludable, non-rival (e.g. Not provided by market)
Consumers lack full knowledge (e.g. Wrong quantity consumed)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Market failure means the market has completely collapsed and no goods are being produced. Correct: Market failure doesn't mean no market exists — it means the market produces the WRONG quantity. cards.front: Externalities: Private and Social Costs and Benefits
cards.back: Market failure occurs when the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently, producing too much or too little of a good. The most common cause is externalities — costs or benefits that fall on third parties not involved in the transaction. A negative externality occurs when the social cost of production or consumption exceeds the private cost. For example, a UK factory that pollutes a river
